Run an Optimizer From Many Starting Points

Source: R/multistart.R
multistart.Rd

Wraps any optimizer and runs it from several starting points, returning the best result together with the number of distinct optimal values reached. Two runs count as reaching the same optimum when their objective values differ by at most distinct_tol. A count above one shows that the surface has more than one local minimum; a count of one does not exclude other minima with the same value or minima that all the starts missed.

Usage

multistart(
  optimizer,
  n = 10,
  starts = NULL,
  spread = 1,
  ncores = NULL,
  distinct_tol = 1e-06,
  verbose = FALSE,
  refresh = 1,
  keep_trace = TRUE
)

Arguments

optimizer

The optimizer() to run, any of them, including another multistart(). Anything else raises an error naming bfgs() as an example.

n

How many starts, the caller's own par among them. Defaults to 10. It becomes the maxit of the wrapper, so n = 0 is rejected with an error that names maxit.

starts

An optional matrix of starting points, one per row, used verbatim; n and spread are then ignored and n is taken from the number of rows. A matrix whose number of columns differs from the length of par is rejected when the run starts, with an error whose message gives the required number of columns.

spread

How widely the random starts are scattered, in units of the unconstrained scale. Defaults to 1.

ncores

The number of processes over which to spread the starts. Defaults to NULL, meaning min(n, max(1, parallel::detectCores() - 2)). Pass 1 for a sequential run. For a deterministic inner optimizer the answer does not depend on the value; for a stochastic one, such as sa(), it does.

distinct_tol

Objective values differing by less than this count as the same optimum. Defaults to 1e-6.

verbose

Report each start as it finishes? Defaults to FALSE. Only a sequential run reports; a run over several processes prints nothing.

refresh

Report every this many starts. Defaults to 1.

keep_trace

Keep the per-start summary? Defaults to TRUE, unlike every other optimizer, because here the trace is one row per start, not one per iteration.

Value

An S7 object of class MultiStart, inheriting from optimizer(), to be handed to minimize().

What the result reports

The result has the par, value, gradient, converged and criterion_met of the best run. Its counts are the sums over all successful starts, its iterations is the number of starts, and its message and trace are those of the wrapper. The summary of the starts is in trace, one row for each start, with the columns start, value, converged and iterations. The message counts the starts that succeeded and those that converged, the distinct optimal values found and how often the best was reached, as in

12 starts, 12 succeeded, 12 converged, 2 distinct optima;
the best was found 6 times.

The count is computed by sorting the values reached and cutting wherever consecutive ones differ by more than distinct_tol.

Starting points

Unless starts is given, the first starting point is par, and the remaining \(n - 1\) form a Latin hypercube: the range of each coordinate is divided into equal strata and each stratum is used exactly once, which spreads the starts more evenly than independent draws. They are generated on the unconstrained scale and mapped back through the bounds, so every start is admissible by construction, however tight the box. The rows of a matrix given in starts are not checked against the bounds in advance: a row outside the box fails in its own run and is recorded as a failed start.

Parallel execution

The starts are independent and are run over ncores processes. The function creates the workers, loads the package, assigns the random streams and shuts the workers down internally: on Unix-alikes the workers are forks, on Windows they form a socket cluster. If the workers cannot load optimizers7, the run gives a warning and proceeds sequentially. If optimizers7 was loaded from source with pkgload, the starts are run sequentially on every platform, without a warning, because a worker would load an installed copy of the package instead of the copy in this session.

Processes are used because the stopping rule is an R object evaluated at every iteration, and R cannot be called from several threads.

The starting points are drawn in the calling session before dispatch, and each worker receives a random stream derived from the seed of the session, so set.seed() reproduces the run. When the inner optimizer is deterministic, such as bfgs() or nelder_mead(), the result is the same for every value of ncores. When the inner optimizer draws random numbers, such as sa(), the result depends on the assignment of the streams to the workers, and therefore on ncores.

Failed starts

A start where the objective is undefined is recorded as failed and the others proceed; the message then reports how many succeeded and quotes the first failure. An error is raised only when every start fails, and it quotes the first error.

References

McKay, M. D., Beckman, R. J. and Conover, W. J. (1979). A comparison of three methods for selecting values of input variables in the analysis of output from a computer code. Technometrics 21, 239–245.

See also

chain() for running optimizers in sequence instead of in parallel, sa() for a global search that needs no restarts, start_runif() for another way of generating starting points.

Examples

multistart(bfgs())
#> <optimizer> multistart (BFGS)
#>   stop when : gradient (max-norm) < 1e-06 or |df| < 1e-10 or |dx| < 1e-08
#>   budgets   : maxit 10, evaluations Inf
#>   settings  : optimizer = BFGS, n = 10, starts = <NULL>, spread = 1, ncores = <NULL>, distinct_tol = 1e-06

# The surface has two minima, and one of them is lower. A single run from the
# origin finds the lower one; the count shows that there is another.
f <- function(p) (p[1]^2 - 1)^2 + p[2]^2 + 0.3 * p[1]
set.seed(1)
r <- minimize(multistart(bfgs(), n = 12), f, c(0, 0))
r@message
#> [1] "12 starts, 12 succeeded, 12 converged, 2 distinct optima; the best was found 6 times. Best run: gradient obtained by finite differences"
table(round(r@trace$value, 6))
#> 
#> -0.305428  0.294146 
#>         6         6 
r@par
#> [1] -1.035579  0.000000

# With a deterministic inner optimizer the answer does not depend on the
# number of processes.
set.seed(11); one  <- minimize(multistart(bfgs(), n = 8, ncores = 1), f, c(0, 0))
set.seed(11); many <- minimize(multistart(bfgs(), n = 8, ncores = 2), f, c(0, 0))
identical(one@value, many@value)
#> [1] TRUE

# A start where the objective is undefined is recorded, not fatal.
g <- function(p) if (p[1] > 0.5) stop("undefined here") else sum(p^2)
set.seed(3)
minimize(multistart(bfgs(), n = 8, ncores = 1), g, c(0, 0))@message
#> [1] "8 starts, 5 succeeded, 5 converged, 1 distinct optimum; the best was found 5 times. First failure: undefined here. Best run: gradient obtained by finite differences"

# If every start fails, the run raises an error that quotes the first
# failure.
try(minimize(multistart(bfgs(), n = 4, ncores = 1),
             function(p) stop("never works"), c(0, 0)))
#> Error : Every start failed. The first error was: never works

# Starting points may be given outright, and then n is the row count.
S <- rbind(c(-2, 0), c(2, 0), c(0, 3))
minimize(multistart(bfgs(), starts = S, ncores = 1), f, c(0, 0))@trace
#>   start      value converged iterations
#> 1     1 -0.3054285      TRUE          5
#> 2     2  0.2941465      TRUE          6
#> 3     3 -0.3054285      TRUE          9
